scenes.title: Is your baby really hungry at night?
scenes.voice: Your baby wakes up four, five, six times a night, and every time, you feed. It feels like she must be hungry. But what if the answer to the night is hiding in the day? In this video I'll show you one number from daytime feeds that explains a lot of night feeds, and why taking away night feeds is usually the wrong first step.

scenes.title: The kitchen that never closes
scenes.sub: A little here, half a bottle there
scenes.voice: Hi, I'm Tetiana, a baby sleep consultant. I've worked with more than five thousand families over eight years. Many moms describe their nights as if the kitchen is open twenty-four seven. The baby wakes, eats a little, falls asleep, and an hour later it all starts again. Mom is exhausted and can't tell where hunger ends and habit begins. And during the day the picture is often like this: a breastfeed here, half a bottle there, a bite of banana on a walk. She seems to eat all the time, but never a proper meal.

scenes.title: The daily food total
scenes.voice: Part one. The daily food total.

scenes.title: Calories move to the night
scenes.body: 600 ml by day + 400 ml by night = the same short gaps
scenes.voice: A child has a daily need for food, and the body tries to meet it. If she eats in small amounts and often during the day, part of the calories moves to the night. Imagine a baby who drinks about a liter of milk a day: six hundred milliliters during the day and four hundred at night, with the same short gaps. For her, the night is just a continuation of the day. She isn't manipulating you and she isn't spoiled. She's catching up.

scenes.title: One number from the day
scenes.voice: Part two. One number from the day.

scenes.title: The gap between feeds
scenes.body: Mostly under 2 to 2.5 hours + more than 3 wakings = catching up at night
scenes.voice: Here's what I look at first: the gap between feeds during the day. If it's mostly shorter than two to two and a half hours, and there are more than three wakings at night, most likely your child is catching up on food at night. Two feeds within forty-five minutes I count as one. The goal for most children after starting solids: four to five proper meals, three to three and a half hours apart.

scenes.title: Why not just drop night feeds
scenes.voice: Part three. Why not just drop the night feeds.

scenes.title: The problem wasn't the night
scenes.body: Under one year, real night feeds can be normal
scenes.voice: Most often, a mom responds by trying to drop night feeds. And the baby really does cry, because she didn't get enough during the day. A few nights like that, and mom decides it's too early. But the problem wasn't the night. And one more important thing: under one year, night feeding can be completely normal. We don't remove real feeds. We remove the snacks that appeared because of the daytime schedule.

scenes.title: A feed or a way to fall asleep?
scenes.voice: Part four. Is it a feed, or a way to fall asleep?

scenes.title: Long and active, or one to two minutes
scenes.body: Keep the real feeds, change the sucking to sleep
scenes.voice: A real feed is long and active: she swallows, she eats, and then falls asleep calmly. If she sucks for a minute or two and drifts off, that isn't about food anymore. It's how she falls asleep. We keep the first, and change the second through the schedule and through how she falls asleep in the evening. Often, once the daytime schedule settles, the night snacks shrink on their own.

scenes.title: Your 3-day plan
scenes.body: Write down every feed with the time, day and night
scenes.voice: For three days, write down everything your child eats, with the exact time, day and night. Count the gaps and the number of night feeds. If most daytime gaps are shorter than two hours, we start with the day: stretch the gaps gradually and make each meal a proper one. At night, keep feeding as before for now.

scenes.title: About your tiredness
scenes.sub: You fed because she asked. That was care.
scenes.voice: A few words about you. Moms who feed five or six times a night often feel they don't have a single minute for themselves, day or night. And when someone says just stop feeding, it sounds like an accusation. But you fed because your child asked, and that was care. Now you're simply changing the timetable of that care: more during the day, calmer at night. Ask your partner to take at least one weekend morning while you keep the food diary for the first days. And don't compare yourself with moms whose baby has slept through since birth. Every child has her own daily need and her own pace.

scenes.title: Your step this week
scenes.body: Three days of a food diary and one number: the daytime gap
scenes.voice: Night feeds aren't the enemy, and they aren't your mistake. But sometimes they're simply a mirror of the day. Your step this week: three days of a food diary, and one number, the gap between daytime feeds. Start with the day, and watch what changes at night.
